en: Preface to the Profound Text on Repentance for the Accomplishment of Practice through the Buddha-Mother Cundī, Reprinted from the Original Woodblocks.
The Bodhisattva Cundī, by virtue of her majestic spiritual power, delivers the multitudes of deluded beings. She extensively proclaims the heart-mantra (*hṛdaya-mantra*);

thus, those of dull faculties and inferior natures obtain the samādhi of fearlessness, subdue demons and enemies, and directly perceive their original nature. How could this be merely a provisional means?
By manifesting great supernatural powers through a single gate, he caused them to obtain blessings—how wonderful! Yet the blessings obtained were truly immeasurable.

My late grandfather, the Duke Xiangyi, upheld this from his youth with a mind that never wavered. Because of it, he rose from the commoner’s robe to attain the highest honors in the imperial examinations.
During the upheaval at Shiming, he escorted the Emperor on the northern expedition; having escaped death a hundred times and traversed ten thousand *li*, he thereafter received profound favor.
Your Excellency, who wears the embroidered robes and wields the majestic battle-axe, has quelled rebellions and pacified both the Chinese and the barbarians.

Although your loyal sincerity is innate, you have consistently received manifest protection during times of peril. For generations, your family line has been adorned with official rank, and successive signs of auspiciousness have appeared.
Your late father, Lord Lanzhai, devotedly maintained the practice of his entire life; he carved the *Cundī-vidhi* and cast and distributed Cundī images.

There were one hundred and eight precious mirrors; though my official rank reached the highest grade, they remained unsullied when dropped into water, and bandits were struck with awe upon encountering them.

I too have followed and upheld them without slackening. Early on, I contemplated the pursuit of the "azure clouds" [official success], yet my father commanded me to inherit his legacy. Thus, by a stroke of fortune, I was mistakenly granted the imperial protection of the Golden Guard (Jinwu).
On the Ren-day of the first month in the year Jia-shen, I dreamed that mountain rocks collapsed and flew away; there was no place left for me to hide, and I heard a voice from the air.
A saying goes: "If you merely hold my mantra, even such calamities cannot avoid you. On the nineteenth day of the third month, the rebel Chén fell upon the capital.
I led my household retainers into street combat; a sharp blade pierced my chest, yet by relying on [the mantra], I suffered no harm.

I fled south on foot, and though I repeatedly encountered bandits, they were unable to harm me. Subsequently, I joined the army of General Ning-nan Hou at Baituntian. As we crossed Lake Dongting, a typhoon...

A wind arose, and the boat was on the verge of capsizing. Thinking he would not escape death, he reflected that his own merit was slight and thin. The Bodhisattva, out of compassion, manifested various signs of harmony with him.

He then made a vow that all sentient beings might together ascend to that Land of Ultimate Bliss. Later, Zhang Gong Wanzhen and Chen Gong Tianzhang succeeded one another as Grand Commissioners of Zhejiang and Fujian;
relying on the benevolence of the Bodhisattva, they were enlightened and guided by him from beneath his banner, thereby achieving their full realization.

The lives of tens of thousands were saved. Both officials merited great praise for their achievements. I personally bestowed upon them the title of Vice Commissioner (Biejia) of Zhangzhou, entrusting them with the task of pacifying and caring for the people.
When the year Renchen arrived, they had only just departed from their posts; three days later, Zhangzhou was besieged. They were unable to avoid the calamity. Judging by this, it is evident.

How could the merit of upholding mantras be anything but profound? Formerly, when I entered Min Province to pay my respects to Master Yinkong at Guangji Temple, I beheld the *Siddhi-ratna-sādhana-praṇidhāna* of Cundī and the painted portraits of the various Dharma-protecting deities; it was something I had never encountered before.

Upon inquiring into the matter, I found it most extraordinary. During the early years of the dynasty, there was a lay practitioner named Xia who worked as a weaver; every night, he was overcome with fear.
He encountered an elderly monk who bestowed upon him a dhāraṇī and a rite of repentance, saying, "If you maintain this, you shall have no fear; you will even be able to explain it.

One day, while he was weaving, his shuttle fell to the ground, yet it returned to his hand; this happened twice more. Suddenly, the generals of the various altars appeared. He prostrated himself and questioned them, and they told him:
Your heart was sincere. The Great Sage commanded me to protect you; thus, I hung a mirror and prayed earnestly to welcome the painters, who then traced the images from within the mirror one by one.
This is the origin of this method of repentance (*poṣadha*). Later, the practitioner passed away while seated; his physical body was enshrined for offerings in Fuzhou.
When I went there to pay my respects, I requested the text of the repentance ritual along with the images and returned with them. This too is a rare occurrence. As for human emotions...
When conditions have not yet been severed, every movement gives rise to transgression. Those who seek to realize Bodhi must first eliminate their past karma;

thus, one knows that the pursuit of merit is itself a source of fault. Only through repentance can one receive the retribution of blessings. For the fundamental awakening is luminously manifest and possesses supernatural powers:
it transforms blazing fires into blue lotuses and turns the ocean of suffering into sweet nectar. This is the power of the Bodhisattva Cundī and the various Dharma-protecting deities.
All these are manifestations of one’s own mind; how could the merit obtained therein be measured? Thus, I have provided the carving blocks so that they may circulate throughout the world.

I pray that those who uphold this mantra and perform repentance will simply realize it directly within themselves. Written on the final day of summer in the year of Renchen by the disciple of the Three Teachings, Xiang Qian, whose Dharma name is Hongci.
With hands washed and incense burned, he respectfully prefaces this work.

(On the Tenth Day of the Fifth Month, the Birthday of Bhagavatī Cundā) Preface to the Precious Repentance Ritual for the Siddhi of the Mother of Buddhas, Cundā, through Incense Offering and Cultivation.
The Daoist Recluse Mo has perused the Tripitaka and found that there are three translations of the *Cundī-sūtra*. The first is titled *The Buddha-Spoken Seven...* [text fragment].
The *Saptakoṭi-Buddhamātṛ-Cittamahācundī-Dhāraṇī Sūtra*, translated by the Śramaṇa Divākara during the Wu Zhou period of the Tang dynasty;

approximately one thousand six hundred characters. Also known as the *Buddhabhāṣita-Saptakoṭi-Buddhamātṛ-Cundī-Maumya-Dhāraṇī Sūtra*, together with the methods for recitation and contemplative practice (*dhyāna-caryā*).
Translated by the Tripitaka Master Vajra from India during the Tang dynasty.

Translated by [Amoghavajra]. Compared with the translation by Śubhakarasiṃha, its wording is approximately six times more extensive. One title is: *The Saptakoṭi-Buddhamātṛ-bhāṣita-Cundī-Dhāraṇī-Sūtra*.

Translated by the Tripiṭaka Master of Daixingshan Monastery, the Śramaṇa of Great Vast Wisdom Amoghavajra, who held the rank of Tèjìn and served as Acting Minister of the Court of State Ceremonial, by imperial decree. Compared with the translation by Vajrabodhi, the wording...

The texts are approximately equal [in number]. However, as the mantras, chapters, and lengths of these scriptures differ vastly, and their phrasing and characters are difficult to reconcile, there is also the *Mahā-saptavidha-buddhamātṛ-hṛdaya-cundī-dhāraṇī* in the Tripitaka edition, which differs in both sound and character from those contained in the three translations.
Furthermore, there is the Tibetan version of the Cundī-dhāraṇī, which again differs even more in its words and phrases. All of these...
These may be consulted for their ornamental presentation, yet they remain subjects for which one should maintain a suspension of judgment.

As for the iconographic layouts, mudrā-seals, Sanskrit script, brushstrokes, the three translations, and the original texts (*śāstramūla*), not a single detail corresponds. Based on a rough assessment of the manifested forms and their preservation, the translation by Amoghavajra is regarded as correct.
Regarding the fundamental body-mudrās, the two translations by Śubhakarasiṃha and Amoghavajra are regarded as correct; however, the Sanskrit characters and...

The phonetic transcriptions have been transmitted with errors and discrepancies; as various editions were carved into printing blocks and circulated, their differences cannot be fully investigated or resolved.

Among those first entered into the canon and distributed for public use, none is more prominent than the *Xianmi Yuntong Chengfo Xinyao Ji* (Collection of the Essential Mind for Attaining Buddhahood through the Perfect Penetration of Exoteric and Esoteric Teachings) in two volumes, upper and lower, by the Song dynasty Dharma Master Daozhi.
It first discusses exoteric cultivation and subsequently discusses esoteric cultivation. Regarding exoteric cultivation, it refers to the practice of Chan meditation.
Regarding the attainment of Buddhahood through realizing one's nature, for those who practice in secret, it is sufficient to focus the mind exclusively on reciting *dhāraṇī* mantras.
By relying on the secret dharma to empower (*adhiṣṭhāna*) the body and mind, one shall swiftly attain the path of Buddhahood, and all that is sought will be fulfilled.

Furthermore, the seven modes of retention and the three secrets are explained in great detail. As for the three secrets: the secret of body is the binding of mudrās; the secret of speech is the recitation of mantras; and the secret of mind...
This constitutes the visualization practice. Furthermore, it is said that Cundī is a Great Dhāraṇī mantra method practiced as an independent division.

It is capable of encompassing all the mantras of the Buddha Family, all the mantras of the Bodhisattvas of the Lotus Family, all the divine mantras of the Vajra Family, all the celestial mantras of the Jewel Family, and all the mantras of the spirits and ghosts of the Karma Family.
Within these five families, each family is further divided into five, resulting in twenty-five families.
Among all mantras, there is none that is not encompassed; yet among all mantras, none encompasses Cundī.
Just as the great ocean can encompass the hundred rivers, while the hundred rivers cannot encompass the great ocean, so it is with this six-syllable wondrously luminous mantra.
It is the subtle and profound original mind of Avalokiteśvara, which is mutually dependent upon Cundī in its sequential order. There are seventy-seven koṭis of Buddhas who, at one and the same time—
Manifesting before us, they proclaim it with one voice. Based on the Sanskrit manuscript of the sutra, it consists of one hundred thousand verses.

Bodhisattva Nāgārjuna verified and established this as the *Vidyādhara-vidhi* (Ritual Manual for the Knowledge-Holders), which has become the primary tradition in China. Regarding other mantras, one must first observe the precepts before being permitted to recite and practice them;

however, as for this mantra, it makes no distinction between the defiled and the pure—one need only maintain it single-mindedly so that those of middling and inferior faculties may easily obtain benefit.
This is called the King of Mantras; it is truly an inconceivable expedient for guiding the deluded.

During the Wanli era, there was the Great Master Jingju Jie, who compiled the *Essential Words of Exoteric and Esoteric Teachings* in one volume. During the Tianqi era, the lay practitioner Qinglian of Guqian, Xie Yujiao, edited the *Cundī Pure Practice* in three volumes.
His preface states that what he has compiled is the "Perfect Interpenetration of the Exoteric and Esoteric."
The essential point is that regarding the method for the initial arrangement of characters, one first performs the recitation and subsequently engages in contemplative practice (*vipaśyanā*).

Furthermore, because multiple characters are difficult to contemplate, they are subsumed under a single character. This single character is the syllable *Lam*, the mantra of the Pure Dharma-realm from the Sanskrit script, which serves as the primary focus.
The non-obstruction between the one and the many is the no small achievement of this compilation concerning the Cundī [Dhāraṇī]. (Cundī Inscription)
Those who have practiced this in past lives are beyond counting; those among the scholar-officials who have maintained it and experienced its miraculous efficacy are likewise beyond counting.

As recorded in the *Jingye* (Pure Deeds): the Court Counselor He Shaolong long maintained this mantra. One night, he dreamed that a youth presented him with robes of nine-petaled flowers, whereupon he was reborn in heaven.
Furthermore, Mr. Yuan Liaofan, the Minister of the Ministry of War, struggled for many years with his success in the imperial examinations.

His own record states: "First, when seeking the provincial examination, I made a vow to complete three thousand good deeds. Next, when seeking advancement to the imperial court, I made a vow to complete ten thousand good deeds.
Ultimately, I took Guanyin Cundi as my standard because I witnessed her spiritual efficacy; thus, one knows that this was not merely a matter of setting one's resolve and practicing virtue."
One who reflects upon themselves to reform their faults and practices skillful means cannot say that the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas speak falsehoods.
For instance, in my own village, the Xiang family lineage has derived power from the *Cundī* mantra-vidyā since the time of Lord Zhong, the late Minister Xiang Yi.
When the Emperor was taken north during the Tumu Incident, the Lord escaped a hundred deaths and achieved great merit, pacifying the rebellion and receiving [the imperial favor].

As for the world’s protection: it reached the Great Jinwu (Palace Guard) Lanzhai Gong Junqing, who braved wind and waves to attend to the imperial carriage and defended the frontier fortresses to attain the highest rank.
His wise successor, Duke Mu Qian, encountered the upheavals that shift mountains and valleys and faced the perils of street-to-street combat against the rebel thieves;
having crossed the hurricane-stricken lake to serve in military garrisons, he consequently left the Jinwu office.
As the Bejia (Vice-Governor) of Jin, he pacified and comforted the people, saving countless lives. When his term ended and he was to untie his official sash, the besieged city remained unharmed.

This was truly because his loyalty and filial piety were deeply rooted through generations, and his literary talent and virtuous conduct were innate. Thus, from his grandfather Xiangyi and his father Jinwu, down to his own tenure as Bejia of Min and Zhangzhou, each generation was able to uphold the practice of Cundi.
Consequently, blessings descended from Heaven, calamities were stilled, and fortune was gathered—this is a clear and great testament of efficacy.
Regarding those whose sincerity is beyond doubt at present: Master Lanzhai devoted his entire life to pious practice;
he had the *Juntishan yigui* (The Ritual Manual of Cundī) carved for publication and cast and distributed precious mirrors of Cundī. His successor, Master Mu, maintained this legacy.

By divine providence, while traveling to Fuzhou, he obtained this *Juntishan fenshu xidi baochan yiwen* (The Precious Liturgy for the Siddhi of Cundī’s Incense Offering and Cultivation), as well as various dharma images and divine diagrams. Regarding these...
The Venerable Monk Yinkong of Guangji Temple—Master Yin—received the transmission from the Daoist Xia of the early Ming dynasty.

He was moved by an old monk who bestowed upon him a text for repentance (*chánwén*), and a celestial deity granted him a mirror-image icon. Later, a true person (*zhēnrén*) sat in meditation until his passing; his physical body (*ròushēn*) is enshrined as an offering in Fuzhou.

This is a particularly inconceivable and great causal connection (*dà yīnyuán*). Master Mu has reverently had it copied, embroidered, and carved into woodblocks, so that it may enter the Tripitaka collection and circulate widely.
It is a thorough understanding that fully manifests the power of great vows—praised by generations for upholding the ancestral legacy—to save the world and benefit sentient beings.
That I, a humble practitioner, have been granted the opportunity to behold and offer praise for this work is surely no small karmic connection regarding my own devotion to Cundī.
Since the year of Gengxu, at the age of twenty-one, when I encountered Master Xueqiao at Mount Jing while he was establishing the Qianzhi Hermitage, I have had faith in her.
Dharma Master Beilin was staying in a mountain hermitage behind the hall. He was accustomed to writing Sanskrit script using a bamboo pen shaped like a comb or brush.
When he was asked to transcribe the Cundī Dhāraṇī, he produced the characters with complete mastery, both vertically and horizontally; the resulting manuscript was exceptionally authentic.
He was also instructed in the Sanskrit pronunciation of the *visarga* (the "two-conjoined" retroflex sound). At that time, he received the transmission from Master Yunqi.

After three years had passed, he finally understood the meaning of the *visarga*. Upon returning, he inscribed the Sanskrit characters upon stone and enshrined them within the Mahayana Hall of the Three Pagodas.
He maintained this practice for six years, until the sixth month of the Bingchen year, when the miracle of the beam’s birth occurred.

Verification: At that time, while he was residing at the head of a catalpa tree by the Bodhisattva Bridge at the North Gate, he was lying on a bamboo mat within a large building during the summer heat.
Suddenly, three bays of the building collapsed simultaneously. Massive beams, massive rafters, massive bricks, and massive tiles were piled up and fell in ruin;

yet he turned them so as to use three great beams as a protective shelter. These beams were all no more than an inch away from his body. When shards of tile struck his person, they felt as light as a sheet of paper.
On another occasion, I merely recited mantras in a loud voice. After a long time, I emerged as if from a dream;
there was not even the slightest harm to my skin. This was an event from when I was twenty-seven years old.

It happened that this winter, National Teacher Hanshan came eastward to Mount Jing to cremate the Venerable Zibo and enshrine his remains in a stupa behind Jizhao Hermitage. I hurried back there immediately.
I relied on this to obtain the verses of the "Bequeathed Teachings to Liang Sheng," which led to my changing my name.

Hearing that my fellow practitioners—Zi Jiang, Yan Yinchi, and Yan Shengsheng—had heard that I had attained power through the practice of *vidyā* (mantra) after surviving a death and rebirth, they joined together to arrange a great offering at the Jingci Zongjing Hall in Wulin.
They invited Master Han to expound the *Cundī-dhāraṇī* practice for receiving and upholding. When Master Han ascended the hall, he spoke with great intensity...
Having bestowed the universal prophecy, he entered the chamber again and showed him the mudrā of the fundamental body (*mūlakāya*), granting him the hand-seal (*hasta-mudrā*) for transmission.
This was firm and utterly distinct. He further showed him the gate of contemplation on the nine sacred Brahmī characters, causing them to be subsumed within the single character *laṃ*.
He also showed him the Brahmī sound of the syllable *oṃ*, making a roar like a hungry tiger swallowing its prey, shaking the mountains and peaks until his breath was exhausted.

The single character "Lan" (藍) is pronounced with the mouth closed, the tongue curled back, and a nasal resonance, like the angry exclamation "Du! of a powerful man; it is a departing tone (去聲), not a level tone (平聲). It is further said:
"If one simply maintains a heart of sincere resolve, even an impure place will immediately become pure. One must not allow this to be interrupted for even a single day;
otherwise, a thousand days would be insufficient to compensate for it. As for the ten days of fasting, these are the days for the Cundi fast; these too must not be missed."

If it is interrupted for even a single day, it cannot be made up for in a thousand days. For lay practitioners living at home, whose five desires are thick and heavy, this one gateway is the most effective for gaining power.
This was the personal oral prediction of Master Han (Zhuhong). His physical body remains present at Caoxi today, and those who come to offer incense all call him the Seventh Patriarch.
At that time, there were over forty men and women among the commoners who received and upheld [the precepts]; in the end...
Over forty years have passed now, and among those who have maintained this practice according to the Dharma without interruption for even a single day, there has been only one person:
the monk Dao-ren. Once, while returning home late at night by boat from Xuan-gong Bridge in the village—commonly known as You-zhang, which is very deep—the boat fell into the water beside him.
After a long time, he emerged with his clothes soaked. This occurred at Yanzi Ji on the Great River, commonly known as Yejitou.
The most perilous moment was when the wind shifted and the boat struck a rock; it was on the verge of breaking apart and sinking, yet he managed to obtain a plug of cloth and escape.

Later, while traveling on the swift current of the Northern Yeh River in Dezhou, bandits forced him into their boat and pointed blades at him. They retreated several paces together, then forced him out of the boat and pushed him into the middle of the river.
Suddenly, he reached the opposite bank with water barely wetting his feet. The bandits departed, and he returned to his boat in haste.
The rapids were a hundred feet deep. There was a youth named Yongjun who plunged into them without a trace. At that time, he knew only to recite mantras and nothing else;

he traversed perilous terrain as if it were level ground, and it would be impossible to describe it all in detail. For instance, during the military upheavals of the year Wuyou (1655), there was a garden on Mount Yaoshan between the East and West Pagodas where a sandalwood image of Cundī was enshrined for worship.
Suddenly, the mountain retreats were consumed by fire, and the calamity of the conflagration left nothing behind.
[Fragmentary]... A solitary image, one went forth and one returned; it was as if a deity presided over it. It is now still enshrined at the Jizhin Pavilion (Ji-zhen Ge) on Mount Yan.
Furthermore, when Master Jingyi of Ding Yuankong was a layman, he once had me, based on a translation by Amoghavajra, paint an image of Cundī in the garden of Mount Yao.
On the day the eyes were opened (*kaiguang*), there suddenly appeared a relic (*gudong*).

The family [of donors] provided an old red ivory axis inscribed with the Cundī Dhāraṇī in Sanskrit script, a Sanskrit-scripted ancient ceramic incense burner, and a copper incense box to assist in the preparation, performance, and offering of the rite;
all of which evoked inconceivable phenomena. On this day, the Mid-Autumn Festival, Grand Master Xueqiao opened the hall at Dongta Temple.
Upon visiting and observing, he sighed in admiration, saying: "What a magnificent realm of Dharma (dharmadhātu) this Sanskrit dhāraṇī constitutes! Thereupon, it was completed.
There were two monks, with several hundred harmonious followers. Master Yuan was refined in the principles of Chan meditation and was skilled in both seal-script and clerical calligraphy.
Because he had resided in this garden for a long time, he compiled for me the various details of the Cundī Dharma-gate.

He transcribed them by hand into a volume that accumulated to nearly an inch in thickness, titled *The Chapter on Entering the Inconceivable Dharma-gate*. Furthermore, the colophon states: "If one can realize this..."
At the time of the secret dharma-gate, one immediately responds with inconceivable wisdom within all daily experiences and objective realms.
Without precepts, there is naturally the precept; without giving, there is naturally giving. Thus it continues until: without wisdom, there is naturally wisdom;

without the myriad practices, there are naturally the myriad practices; without the three minds, there are naturally the three minds. Therefore, this is for the sake of accomplishing the inconceivable dharma-gate. It is not...
This is the stage of traversing kalpas, wherein one manifests as a Buddha. Master Jingyi has explained the meaning in this manner, and I have preserved it with great care.
Furthermore, I have previously transcribed and carved the *Cundī-sādhana* on several occasions:
once as a postscript to the Sanskrit text of the *Cundī-praṇidhāna-vidhi* for the śramaṇa Hongbi of Sheng’en Temple in Wumen, and once for those who share the same [spiritual] reliance.
Lin Taishi Renxian of Ruian composed the Preface to the *Zhunti ji shuo* (Explanations of the Zhunti Collection).
Liu Xin Jingyuyue of Mian, Sichuan, compiled the *Zhunti yuan*, also titled the *Jingyin ji* (Collection on Pure Causes), which was transmitted by Min Xue-xian Hongfu of Shaoshan.

Regarding the prefaces for the woodblock editions: one was written by Zhang Taishi Shou'an, a fellow resident of Kuaiji, for the compilation of the *Zhunti zhangguo* (The Fruits of Holding the Name of Cundī) by Mei Zhonghan Shengsheng and Shisheng of Xuancheng;
another was a preface to the *Zhunti chihufa* (Method for Holding the Name of Cundī) composed by Master Suhua Xu;
and a third was for the *Jianyichi song* (Simple and Easy Recitation) compiled by Zhou Bangtai of Siming.
The Dharma was established by Chan Master Ruohan. It was printed and prefac-ed by Feng Zongzhen, Zi Yuanyuanhuai.

Furthermore, Zhou Zhongcheng Yuanliang and Lianggong, along with his younger brother Liangjie of Central China, composed a preface for the concurrent circulation of the three translations of the Cundī Sūtra.
Generally speaking, all these editions are based on the "Perfect Penetration of the Exoteric and Esoteric," though they have been subject to intentional deletions and additions. As for their...
This means that one must be pure to become enlightened and enter through faith; this is true of all Buddhadharma, not just the Cundī-dhāraṇī.
As for enabling people to transcend the triple world and hasten toward Bodhi, for the benefit of both self and others, nothing possesses such manifest efficacy as Cundī.
She is truly what is called an "extraordinary expedient. Some may say that those who hold the Cundī-dhāraṇī fulfill their hopes through indirect means.
If one harbors a mind of aversion, then reciting the Buddha’s name is a hope for rebirth in the Pure Land, and practicing Zen meditation is a hope for awakening to the Way.

In the Perfect Teaching (Enshū) and the Esoteric Teachings (Mikkyō), the application of these capacities is identical. The *Avalokiteśvara Commentary* states: "Though one seeks in every thought-moment, there is no characteristic of a seeker or that which is sought;
this is the method of contemplation. To spread the wheel-moon within the single mind and to settle the bright jewel within all phenomena—this is precisely my [practice].

"Master, 'washing the mind and withdrawing into the profound'—the meaning of this, as well as 'purifying through fasting and vigilance to clarify the spirit of one's virtue,' cannot be discussed on the same level as the various other mantras and their accomplishments.
In the year Wuchen (1868), when I, the monk Sǎo, received my official appointment at the capital, I maintained a very close relationship with the elder Xiáng of Lánzhāi.
Together, we verified and finalized the *Cundī-vidhi* that was to be carved into woodblocks."
Furthermore, he was able to receive from the late sovereign, Duke Mu, the profound patterns of the dark mysteries, which were truly rare and extraordinary.
On the sixth day of this second month, he went forth from the Xiang clan to shave his head and don the robes of ordination, becoming a Bodhisattva who dwells amidst the dust of the world.

To inaugurate this unprecedented and most excellent place of practice, a repentance altar was established at Taiping Hermitage by Xianxi, where many monastics and laypeople gathered for a time to offer their words of praise.
Each family shall compose a verse on the Three-Eyed, Eighteen-Armed Cundī.
Thus, the wondrous fruition of Cundī is woven as both warp and woof, from beginning to end; herein lies the dhāraṇī that encompasses the five great sections.

It is here that the ancestral legacy of the Duke Xiangyi is sanctified, and the prudent planning for future generations is preserved. This humble mendicant has specifically revealed this for the sake of all beings.

On an auspicious occasion at dawn, I have composed this to manifest the supernatural powers of Cundī and to exhort you all to chant and recite it; may it serve as a brief manual for the upholding of the Dharma by my fellow practitioners.
This is merely a drum-roll for the propagation of this entire Dharma-gate.
Composed on the first day of the second month of the spring in the Dingyou year of the Shunzhi era by the lay devotee Tan Zhengmo of Bān-tán (pseudonym Fuzheng Dao-yi),
a disciple who upholds the teachings of the Patriarch Han from Caoxi,
a descendant of Zixiao Feixian and former Jinshi of the second rank in the Wuchen year, at the age of sixty-eight.
Preface to the Ritual for Cultivating Repentance of the Buddha-Mother Cundī.
Contemplating the people and things of the world, there are none who do not possess this numinous mind.

Within the *dharmadhātu*, due to the various causes that draw forth and evoke [their responses], there arise all manner of distinctions that intermingle, forming this pattern of ordinary beings and sages. And as for the Buddha...

The Sages established their teachings to benefit sentient beings by each guiding and inspiring them according to what they are inclined toward, causing them to individually examine their origins and return to their ultimate end so as not to lose the correctness of their own nature and disposition.
Furthermore, there are the skillful means of both worldly and world-transcending dharmas; as for the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas, they fill the dust motes of all lands, yet [they remain] alone...
There is Avalokiteśvara and Cundī, whose salvation of the world is most efficacious and miraculous.

Furthermore, within the Dharma-realm, there is not a single person who does not know of Avalokiteśvara and Cundī. This is precisely because Cundī is the manifestation of the Universal Gate (Samantamukha) of Avalokiteśvara.
Not seeing her mantra, [the text] first places the Mantra of the Sublime and Radiant King (Avalokiteśvara) at its head.
The Cundī Dhāraṇī concludes this section. This mantra is, in fact, the sovereign samādhi within the secret treasury of the Dharma-realm;
it is capable of giving rise to the adornments of wisdom and virtue of all Buddhas and Bodhisattvas. For this reason, it is called the "Mother of Buddhas."
Based on this, one aligns with the sentiments of both ordinary beings and sages, and upholds the nature of Vairocana. This is the mirror-seal of the Lord of Lords.
Because these Bodhisattvas possess the resolve to inevitably save others, sentient beings possess the conviction to inevitably seek them out.

Were there no such resonance between response and stimulus, there would be none within the entire Dharma-realm who would be willing to believe and accept [this teaching]. This applies equally to the recitation of mantras and the mindfulness of the Buddha.
The same applies here; however, there is a slight difference in the case of Chan meditation. In the recitation of mantras, faith is paramount; in Chan, doubt is the starting point.

When faith reaches its peak, one becomes free of doubt and enters directly. When doubt reaches its peak, one inevitably attains faith and achieves sudden penetration. In the practice of mantra-recitation and Buddha-recitation, doubt is absolutely forbidden.
To have even the slightest doubt is like entering the fray with a whirling blade while lacking martial resolve; one will surely bring about one's own defeat.
Furthermore, although Zen meditation is said to involve "doubt" (*yiqing*), one must first have deep faith in the principle that there is a "special transmission outside the teachings.

It is not that one doubts whether this [transmission] exists or does not exist, or whether it is uncertain; rather, it is the intense desire to clarify the distinctiveness of the ancients' words and phrases that constitutes the doubt.
If one were to doubt in such a manner [as mere uncertainty], that would instead represent the height of faith.
Seeking it with such urgency—how could there be any difference between its beginning and its end? Within this, there are two meanings.
First, it is beneficial for the ignorant, because their minds are free from distracting thoughts; yet one fears they may lack the will to seek.

If they possess the will to seek, then the secret treasury shall be opened, and its natural brilliance will shine forth. Second, it is a warning against the clever, because their minds are prone to great distraction. Not...

One must be able to focus the mind with singular intensity. If one can achieve such single-mindedness, then the entire Dharma-realm will be fully encompassed, and the true permanence of the essence will be revealed.

For this reason, even those as simple and unrefined as Yan Hui and Zeng Shen were uniquely able to receive the mind-to-mind transmission, whereas those as literary and refined as You Zi and Xia Hou could hardly enter the inner chamber.
How much more so when holding this mantra, which alone serves to gather and restrain the wandering minds of body, speech, and mind within the three marks [of impermanence, suffering, and non-self]?

Who would say that Buddhism does not correspond with the sacred learning of the sages? If this is so, then for the Confucian tradition, it is sufficient simply to practice self-mastery and vigilance in solitude;
why must one additionally recite Buddhist mantras? It is said: From of old, the various Confucian scholars have devoted themselves exclusively to the affairs of worldly instruction, yet...
They are unwilling to seek a breakthrough within the nature of their own body and mind.
Yet, when they encounter the perils of birth and death—amidst water, fire, or the blade—who among them has attained the functional application of great supernatural power and liberation?

This is precisely because their will does not lie in birth, death, or the preservation of life; therefore, by means of this mantra’s power, they are guided toward it. If there were another transmission, [it would be] great.

Medicine can cure ten thousand ailments, yet it must necessarily have a "medicinal guide" (yao-yin) before it can reach the five viscera and six bowels, and penetrate the twelve channels and networks, thereby addressing wind, cold, heat, and dampness, as well as conditions of the exterior and interior, or deficiency and repletion.

Without this guide, the medicine would remain obstructed and unable to reach its destination on its own. For this reason, Cundī is called the "Mother of Buddhas," for she is like a mother who can save her child.
If the child can seek out the mother, then both will be found. If the child does not single-mindedly seek the mother, then the mother will merely stand by her gate in sorrow.
The destination reached by the aspirations of all people in the world is precisely where the medicinal guide reaches;
therein lies the restoration of health and longevity, the shedding of the old skin and transformation of the bones, and the resurrection from the dead to transcend the mundane.
This transcends the holy. Furthermore, it depends on the depth of one's cultivation and the courage of one's resolve.

Moreover, the dull-witted may fall into a state of neither indignation nor aspiration, or be led astray by the five desires; the intelligent may fall into a mind of theft and fleeting glances, or be deluded by heterodox views.
Thus, there may be seeking that does not concern life and destiny, or there may be upholding that lacks single-mindedness and constancy.
It is absolutely impossible to realize the truth without seeking the True Dharma.

With a sincere heart, I take refuge and pay homage to the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Cchittvika, the Greatly Compassionate and Greatly Merciful One.
O Holy Cchittvika, Great Bodhisattva! Your wrathful and wondrous form shakes the eight directions;
The flames from your crimson heart terrify all hundredfold evils. I, your disciple, with a single mind, take refuge and pay homage.
With a sincere heart, I take refuge and pay homage to the Bodhisattva Mahāsattvā Ārya Mārīcī.
Ārya Mārīcī, Great Bodhisattva, To you who were born as the beloved son of five hundred deities,
The True Youth who follows the Holy Body— I, your disciple, with a single mind, take refuge and pay homage.
With a sincere heart, I take refuge and pay homage to the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Gandharva King of Great Compassion.
Gandharva King, Great Bodhisattva: Subduing demons, realizing the nature, manifesting the golden body, leopard crown, dragon-sword, and majestic elephant;
Disciple, with single-minded devotion, takes refuge and pays homage.
With a sincere heart, I take refuge and pay homage to the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva, the Lord of the Consecration Division, who is endowed with great kindness and great compassion.
Lord of the Consecration Division, Great Bodhisattva: You extensively bestow ambrosia to nourish all sentient beings;
May the faithful of the ten directions all receive your refreshing rain. Disciple, with a single mind, takes refuge and pays homage.
With a sincere heart, we take refuge and pay homage to the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Vajrapāṇi Kṣitigarbha (Huiji Jingang), the Greatly Compassionate and Greatly Merciful One.
Vajrapāṇi Kṣitigarbha, Great Bodhisattva, Manifesting transformations in all directions, you subdue demons;
Earth, water, fire, and wind all manifest their forms. Disciple, with single-minded devotion, I take refuge and pay homage.
With a sincere heart, I take refuge and pay homage to the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva, the Great Compassionate and Merciful Messenger of the Radiant Snake.

O Messenger of the Radiant Snake, Great Bodhisattva! You who manifest divine power within the Inner Court of Celestial Physicians, dispelling calamities, eliminating illness, and saving all sentient beings—disciple, with a single mind, I take refuge and pay homage to you.
With a sincere heart, I take refuge and pay homage to the Greatly Compassionate and Greatly Merciful Dharma-protecting devas and all the assembly of holy ones.
Dharma-protecting devas and all the assembly of holy ones, Surrounding me from the ten directions to protect this maṇḍala, do not forget your own divisions;
Present your mudrās and mantras, and assist me in propagating the Cundī-dhāraṇī method.
I prostrate and take refuge in Susiddhi (kneeling recitation). With head bowed to the ground, I pay homage to the seven koṭis.
I now praise the Great Cundī; May you, out of compassion, grant your protection.

May the Buddhas, out of their compassion, accept my repentance.
With a sincere heart, I, the disciple [Name], repent:
from time immemorial throughout vast kalpas until this very day, I have been deluded regarding the awakening to non-self.

One calculates that there is a self and a person. Once this calculation of a self has arisen, one constantly clings to what belongs to the self (*ātmīya*). The sense bases and objects swirl about profusely;

consciousness and its aggregates rush to and fro, binding and agitating the body and mind like a flash of lightning. The pure faculties of eye, ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind fail to awaken for even a single thought-moment.
They have instead become the six heretical masters, stealing the wealth of the Dharma King and joining with the bandits of extreme views (*antagrāhadṛṣṭi*).

As these thieves grow ever more rampant, they destroy the city of Nirvāṇa, ravage the Dharma-body (*dharmakāya*), and incinerate the life of wisdom (*prajñājīvita*). Such transgressions as these exceed the sands of the Ganges in number; from delusion to further delusion, they continue on.
I could not fathom its beginning or end; only now do I begin to awaken. I am deeply ashamed and filled with self-reproach, trembling in body and mind with alarm day and night.

Having forever severed delusion and awakening, and abandoned craving for self and others, I cast myself into the city of Nirvana and return to the Land of Peace and Bliss through the realization of non-self.
Having subdued the six heretical teachers, I shall gather the wealth of the Dharma King and receive the treasury of the three jewels. I shall sustain the life of wisdom and augment the Dharma-body;
I shall kindle the lamp of the Dharma-nature to shine eternally and inexhaustibly. My practices, vows, affairs, and principles shall not conflict with the realms of dust.
I vow to extensively protect the Triple Gem and the Three Vehicles. May all sins of delusion and awakening be eliminated through repentance. From this day forth, until I attain Bodhi, may it be so.
Moment by moment they are firm; moment by moment they are diligent. Their body and mind are autonomous, and their eloquence is unimpeded. Within a single thought-moment, they possess all-knowledge.
One must understand that while all phenomena are ultimately empty and quiescent, they constantly deliver and liberate all sentient beings.
They realize nirvāṇa together, yet they do not take nirvāṇa as something to be realized.

Having finished the repentance, with a sincere heart take refuge and pay homage to the eternally abiding Triple Gem.
With a sincere heart, make this vow:
"May all the fruits of the various good deeds that I have cultivated, through the power of my prostrations, recitations, and repentance..."
I dedicate this to all sentient beings, that they may transcend the suffering of the three realms and swiftly realize enlightenment.
May it return to me what I have sought and assist in the accomplishment of supreme siddhi.
Having made this dedication of aspiration, I take refuge with a sincere heart and pay homage to the eternally abiding Triple Gem.
I take refuge in all Tathāgatas (one prostration for each four-line verse): May the Buddhas of the five wisdoms and ten bodies,
together with all sentient beings,
Enter the Vajradhātu and take refuge in the Supreme Vehicle, The Yoga Secret Teachings.

Enter the Vajradhātu and take refuge in the irreversible Bodhisattva Saṅgha of great compassion;
May I, together with all sentient beings, Enter the Vajradhātu.
Having taken refuge in the Triple Gem, I dedicate all merits to all sentient beings so that we may together accomplish the Unsurpassed Path.
Above, I have prostrated to the Great Cundī Bodhisattva; herein lies the "Mystical Text on Repentance for the Accomplishment of Refinement. May its merit be perfected.
May it be fulfilled. May these boundless roots of goodness sprinkle and moisten all realms as numerous as grains of sand. Homage to the assembly of noble ones.

(When the practitioner enters contemplation and recites, they should first understand that the Buddhas, sentient beings, and their own mind are one and the same perfect luminosity. Vertically exhaustive and horizontally pervasive, this single present thought-moment is complete and without deficiency; it is non-dual and undifferentiated, yet it constantly abides in a most profound state.

With compassion for all sentient beings, they should bring about *siddhi* through the correspondence of the three secrets. Although there are many visualizations shown within the practice of recitation, none exceed those of the Sanskrit syllables and the sound of the mantra, whether in their general or specific characteristics. Furthermore...)

Distant from the observer and the observed, the grasper and the grasped, and every single phenomenon and principle—all are the inconceivable, secret realm of reality. If one practices and maintains this way, why worry that the fruit of Buddhahood will not be perfected, that karmic obstacles will not be extinguished, or that *siddhi* will not be attained?
In the late summer of the Renchen year of the Shunzhi era, the Buddha’s disciple Xiang Qian, whose Dharma name is Hongci, reverently copied [this work] from Sanyuan in Min and,
having purified himself through ritual bathing, engraved it anew.
